analysis.one_liner: Strips medical malpractice insurers of their exemption from antitrust laws against price fixing.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have ended a federal antitrust exemption for medical malpractice insurers, got a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing but never a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: A 1945 federal law called the McCarran-Ferguson Act lets insurance companies share information and set rates together without being treated as an illegal monopoly. This bill would carve medical malpractice insurance out of that exemption, making it illegal for commercial insurers to fix prices, rig bids, or divide up markets in that line of insurance. State insurance regulators would still be allowed to gather data and set rates themselves. The bill never came to a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Doctors and hospitals paying medical malpractice premiums, and ultimately their patients, if competition among insurers would lower premiums. The bill's premise, laid out in hearings, was that concentrated insurers could legally coordinate on rates under the McCarran-Ferguson exemption, and that exposing them to antitrust law would push premiums toward competitive levels [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Makes price fixing, bid rigging, and market allocation by commercial medical malpractice insurers subject to federal antitrust law, which is currently blocked by the McCarran-Ferguson Act's insurance exemption [S2][S3].
The Senate Judiciary Committee, chaired at the time by the bill's sponsor Sen. Leahy, held a hearing on the issue (S.Hrg. 109-557), putting the insurers' rate-setting practices on the record [S5].

analysis.who_pays: Commercial medical malpractice insurers, who would lose the legal ability to coordinate on pricing and market division; if coordination is one reason premiums are high, insurers' margins could shrink as competition increases [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: Insurers argue the McCarran-Ferguson exemption supports industry-wide data sharing and loss forecasting that keeps a volatile line of insurance stable; repealing it for malpractice coverage could reduce that stability without guaranteeing lower premiums, since premium swings are driven largely by claim outcomes and investment returns [S2].

The bill targets only malpractice insurance, so any savings would be limited to that one market, and the bill was a single-chamber, one-page measure that left unresolved how courts would treat existing shared-information arrangements [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If coordinated pricing is part of why malpractice premiums rose sharply in the early 2000s, exposing insurers to antitrust law is a low-cost way to discipline the market, and it leaves state regulators' rate-setting untouched [S2][S3]. The honest caveat is that the bill's effect on premiums is unproven — premium levels in this market are heavily driven by lawsuit outcomes, and repealing the exemption would be a bet that competition, not regulation, is the better check. It never got far enough for anyone to find out.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which held a hearing, but the bill was never voted on and died when the 109th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Leahy introduced the bill on July 28, 2005, joined by nine Democratic colleagues, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee [S1][S5].
On June 20, 2006, the Judiciary Committee held a hearing on the subject, printed as S.Hrg. 109-557, but never reported the bill to the full Senate [S5].
No further action was taken, and the bill expired when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Commercial medical malpractice insurers kept the McCarran-Ferguson antitrust exemption, retaining the ability to coordinate on pricing and market division without federal antitrust exposure. Doctors and patients saw no change in how malpractice insurance is priced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Malpractice insurers kept their antitrust exemption

sides.party_line_note: All 10 cosponsors, including the sponsor, were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill died in committee without a recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill would end their McCarran-Ferguson antitrust exemption for malpractice coverage, exposing price fixing, bid rigging, and market allocation to federal antitrust enforcement. By dying, the bill left the insurers' ability to coordinate on rates and divide markets intact.

The bill only covers malpractice insurance, but it would have been a precedent for narrowing the industry-wide McCarran-Ferguson exemption, which insurers defend as essential to shared loss data and rate stability. Nothing happened, so the broader exemption was untouched.
They pay malpractice premiums, which was the bill's core concern; with the bill dead, they continue to face premiums set in a market where insurers may lawfully coordinate.
